From Okiep to the World

By: Liz Fish | Commission

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
It’s a beautiful story, inspiring and quintessential South African stories in one of the most far-flung unlikely places.

Unique Selling Point:
Okeip, Nababeep and Springbok- when one hears those names one thinks of small, stark, and desperately poor towns far up the West Coast. Okiep-a dusty mining town best known for the deserted copper mine who’s toxic dust still blows across the houses - is a tumble weeds roll away from Springbok. But today its being put back on the map by the Garage Contemporary Dance Ensemble. They have just returned from Germany after performing at Ruhrtriennale 2025 Premiere- this is on the back of many other successful European performances.


Summary:
But in the words of the founder Alfred Henkell these shows are just to raise money- their real audiences are in Springbok, Okiep, Nabaeep - that is who they care about. They have grown these audiences through screening their films and performing their craft to over 500 paying residences. They are telling their story and growing their passion in these far flung towns and they are a riot of pride and recognition. That’s who they are doing it for.
Alfred Henkel and John Linden legends in the contemporary dance world retired to their hometown Okiep. They had spent decades developing contemporary dance in Cape Town, establishing the Jazzart Dance Theatre into South Africa’s premier performing arts training and performance institution since 1986.
Alfred also establish dance as a subject in schools across the Cape Flats and its one of his prodigies Byron Klaasens that is the now the Artistic Director of the Garage Dance Ensemble – ironically he was also born in Okiep although he started dancing in Cape Town in one of the Flats schools
But retirement was boring and Alfred and John once again they found themselves on the dance floor – or rather in the garage and re-egnited a group they had establish in the 80’s - Die Namakwalandse Dans Geselskap – based in the small towns of Nababeep and Okiep in the Northern Cape.
Brandon grew up with his grandmother who taught him reel dance, Stoff dance, sakkie and Langarm- all deeply rooted in these communities. So, tapping into this deep well of dance they have woven it into their contemporary dance using a local actress to narrate their stories.

Further information:
In the beginning they were tales of their exploitation from the mines and colonialism, but Brandon says they have got this protest theatre out of their system- now they want to tell stories of joy, of being proudly coloured, proudly nama and not to be pitied. His latest choreography “Gat” is to remind coloured people of their roots and to celebrate who they are.
And they have a lot to celebrate- these are no amateur performances – they powerful- performed outside in the dust, properly lite with theatre lights and a good sound system and emotive strong bodies.
But drawing the community in is critical- they run keep fit classes in the evening for the tannies and classes for the kids on Saturdays. Alfred now in his early 70’s still teaches but no longer performs. But he is an excellent fund raiser with extensive networks and for his sins he is still writing funding proposals. They are one of the few who received their money from Lotto.
I have access to professionally filmed performances and films, and a beautiful archive of community performances. They are performing at Die Woord Fees in Stellenbosch in early October which will be filmed.


Extra Budget Items:
Its a 6 hour road trip from Cape Town so will need two travel days from the crew and presenter

Alfred Henkel and John Linden legends in the contemporary dance world retired to their hometown Okiep. They had spent decades developing contemporary dance in Cape Town, establishing the Jazzart Dance Theatre into South Africa’s premier performing arts training and performance institution since 1986. Alfred also establish dance as a subject in schools across the Cape Flats and its one of his prodigies Byron Klaasens that is the now the Artistic Director of the Garage Dance Ensemble – ironically he was also born in Okiep although he started dancing in Cape Town in one of the Flats schools But retirement was boring and Alfred and John once again they found themselves on the dance floor – or rather in the garage and re-egnited a group they had establish in the 80’s - Die Namakwalandse Dans Geselskap – based in the small towns of Nababeep and Okiep in the Northern Cape. Brandon grew up with his grandmother who taught him reel dance, Stoff dance, sakkie and Langarm- all deeply rooted in these communities. So, tapping into this deep well of dance they have woven it into their contemporary dance using a local actress to narrate their stories.
metadata.Further information: In the beginning they were tales of their exploitation from the mines and colonialism, but Brandon says they have got this protest theatre out of their system- now they want to tell stories of joy, of being proudly coloured, proudly nama and not to be pitied. His latest choreography “Gat” is to remind coloured people of their roots and to celebrate who they are. And they have a lot to celebrate- these are no amateur performances – they powerful- performed outside in the dust, properly lite with theatre lights and a good sound system and emotive strong bodies. But drawing the community in is critical- they run keep fit classes in the evening for the tannies and classes for the kids on Saturdays. Alfred now in his early 70’s still teaches but no longer performs. But he is an excellent fund raiser with extensive networks and for his sins he is still writing funding proposals. They are one of the few who received their money from Lotto. I have access to professionally filmed performances and films, and a beautiful archive of community performances. They are performing at Die Woord Fees in Stellenbosch in early October which will be filmed.
